title: Clean and search text
goal: Standardize labels and extract useful pieces from text columns.
prerequisites: You can select columns and filter with Boolean masks.

cells.title: Clean spaces and preserve meaningful labels
cells.explanation: The `.str` accessor applies text operations to each entry in a Series. `strip()` removes spaces at the beginning and end. A label map can then standardize spelling while preserving the exact labels you want.
cells.code:
df = raw_students()
df["Name"] = df["Name"].astype("string").str.strip()
result = df.loc[df["Student_ID"] == "S001", ["Student_ID", "Name"]]
print(result)

questions.answer: Leading and trailing whitespace from each text value.

questions.prompt: Will strip remove the space inside a two-word name?

cells.task: Standardize all Campus labels as exactly RAK or Dubai. Handle case and surrounding spaces before mapping. Store Student_ID and the cleaned Campus for every source row in result.
cells.solution:
df = raw_students()
campus_text = df["Campus"].astype("string").str.strip().str.lower()
df["Campus"] = campus_text.map({"rak": "RAK", "dubai": "Dubai"})
result = df[["Student_ID", "Campus"]]
print(result)
cells.solution_note: S002 changes from dubai to Dubai. The abbreviation RAK remains uppercase.

options: It would remove the whole value
check.feedback: A known-label map is useful when abbreviations require special capitalization.

cells.watch: An unrecognized value passed through a dictionary map becomes missing; inspect unmatched labels.
cells.takeaway: Standardize categories without destroying their meaning.

cells.title: Literal text and regular expressions
cells.explanation: `str.contains()` checks whether text contains a pattern. Use `regex=False` when you want the characters literally. With a regular expression, characters such as a dot can have special meanings.
cells.code:
files = pd.Series(["report.csv", "reportXcsv", "notes.csv", None, "csv.backup"], dtype="string")
mask = files.str.contains(".csv", regex=False, na=False)
result = files[mask]
print(result)

questions.prompt: Why does the code set regex=False?
questions.answer: The dot should be an actual dot, not a pattern matching any character.
It treats a missing text entry as not matching the search.

cells.task: Select all nonmissing filenames that begin with report. Use a regular expression and store the result.
cells.hint: The ^ symbol anchors a regular expression to the start of the text.
cells.solution:
files = pd.Series(["report.csv", "reportXcsv", "notes.csv", None, "csv.backup"], dtype="string")
mask = files.str.contains(r"^report", regex=True, na=False)
result = files[mask]
print(result)
cells.solution_note: Both report.csv and reportXcsv begin with report. Their extensions do not matter for this question.

check.prompt: Which argument makes a search literal?

cells.watch: Always be clear whether a pattern is literal text or a regular expression.

cells.title: Split a value into separate columns
cells.explanation: `str.split()` separates text at a delimiter. `expand=True` creates separate columns rather than a list in each cell. Limiting splits can protect the rest of a string when a delimiter appears repeatedly.
cells.code:
emails = pd.Series(["amira@example.edu", "bilal@example.edu", None], dtype="string")
result = emails.str.split("@", n=1, expand=True, regex=False)
result.columns = ["Username", "Domain"]
print(result)

questions.prompt: What character divides the email into two parts?
What will the first Username be?

questions.answer: We want two table columns, so each piece can be selected and analyzed separately.

cells.task: Use the same emails. Extract Domain as a Series, then store the frequency of each known domain in result as a value_counts() Series.
cells.hint: Select the second split piece with `.str[1]`, then call `.value_counts()`.
cells.solution:
emails = pd.Series(["amira@example.edu", "bilal@example.edu", None], dtype="string")
domains = emails.str.split("@", n=1, regex=False).str[1]
result = domains.value_counts()
print(result)
cells.solution_note: example.edu has two known occurrences. Missing domains are excluded by value_counts() by default.

check.prompt: What object does expand=True produce here?
check.feedback: The split pieces become columns in a DataFrame.

cells.verify:
assert result.loc[0, "Username"] == "amira"
assert result.loc[1, "Domain"] == "example.edu"
assert result.iloc[2].isna().all()
cells.watch: This is a string-processing exercise, not full validation of every legal email address.
cells.takeaway: Split text into fields before summarizing its parts.

cells.title: Extract only values that match a structure
cells.explanation: `str.extract()` uses capture groups to pull parts out of a matching pattern. Named groups become useful column names. A nonmatching string produces missing fields, which you should inspect.
cells.code:
codes = pd.Series(["AI-101", "IT-205", None, "bad"], dtype="string")
result = codes.str.extract(r"^(?P<Program>[A-Z]+)-(?P<Number>\d+)$")
print(result)

questions.prompt: What do Program and Number name in the pattern?
questions.answer: The two captured fields, which become output columns.

questions.prompt: What happens to the value bad?
questions.answer: Both extracted fields are missing because the whole pattern does not match.
They require the full string to match the structure, rather than accepting a matching piece inside other text.

cells.task: Use the same codes. Extract the fields and convert Number to nullable Int64.
cells.hint: Pass the extracted Number column through `pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce")`.
cells.solution:
codes = pd.Series(["AI-101", "IT-205", None, "bad"], dtype="string")
result = codes.str.extract(r"^(?P<Program>[A-Z]+)-(?P<Number>\d+)$")
result["Number"] = pd.to_numeric(result["Number"], errors="coerce").astype("Int64")
print(result)
cells.solution_note: The valid numeric codes are 101 and 205. The missing and nonmatching source entries remain missing.

check.prompt: Does extract automatically turn captured digits into integers?
options: No; convert the extracted text explicitly
Only when the group has a name
check.feedback: Matching digits is different from choosing a numeric data type.

cells.verify:
assert result.loc[0, "Program"] == "AI"
assert result.loc[1, "Number"] == "205"
assert result["Number"].isna().sum() == 2
cells.solution_verify:
assert str(result["Number"].dtype) == "Int64"
assert result.loc[0, "Number"] == 101
assert result["Number"].isna().sum() == 2
cells.watch: A successful pattern match checks structure, not whether the code exists in an official registry.
cells.takeaway: Extract structured pieces and then assign appropriate types.
